The Federal Government has commenced a £746m modernisation programme for the Lagos Port Complex, Apapa, and Tin Can Island Ports, with the project expected to improve cargo handling, reduce trade costs and generate at least 20,000 direct and indirect jobs. The Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, flagged off the project on Wednesday at a ceremony held at Tin Can Island Port, alongside the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, and other senior government officials. Oyetola’s media aide, Dr Bolaji Akinola, disclosed this in a statement released on Wednesday. The project, valued at approximately N1.45tn, is expected to tackle longstanding infrastructure deficiencies at the two ports, attract more international shipping lines and strengthen Nigeria’s position in regional and global trade. Speaking at the ceremony, Oyetola said the initiative was a major step towards fulfilling President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda through infrastructure development, investment and job creation. He said the country’s growing population and expanding trade had placed enormous pressure on port facilities that were no longer adequate for modern shipping operations. According to the minister, Apapa Port was established in 1913, while Tin Can Island Port was commissioned in 1977, when Nigeria’s population was about 67.2 million, annual trade stood at $17bn and cargo throughput was 8.11 million metric tonnes. He said the country’s population had since increased to about 240 million, merchandise trade had exceeded $100bn annually, while cargo throughput had risen to 129.3 million metric tonnes, almost 16 times the volume recorded when Tin Can Island Port opened. Oyetola said the disparity between the growth in economic activity and the capacity of the ports had made their comprehensive upgrade imperative. “The cost of inaction is far greater than the cost of modernisation,” he added, saying Nigeria would not surrender its competitive advantage. We cannot achieve this ambition with infrastructure that falls behind the demands of modern shipping,” Oyetola said. The minister lamented that cargo dwell time at Nigerian ports had historically ranged from 10 to 18 days, compared with three to five days at leading international ports. He said the delays had resulted in congestion, demurrage and storage charges, with inefficiencies estimated to cost the Nigerian economy as much as $4bn annually. Oyetola warned that Nigeria risked losing maritime business to neighbouring countries that had invested in deep-sea ports and modern cargo-handling facilities. He said the project would cover the rehabilitation of quay walls and berths, dredging and navigation channels, access facilities, cargo-handling equipment and operational systems. It will address longstanding physical constraints while advancing more integrated, efficient and digitally enabled port operations,” Oyetola said. The minister said the construction and related activities would create jobs in engineering, dredging, logistics, transportation, port operations and other sectors. “Our agricultural products, processed foods, solid minerals, manufactured goods, textiles and petrochemical products must compete effectively in regional and global markets. Efficient ports will help exporters meet delivery schedules, reduce costs, preserve product quality and secure international buyers’ confidence. They will equally create a more enabling environment for manufacturers, agro-processors and micro, small and medium-sized enterprises,” he said. To minimise disruptions during construction, Oyetola said he had approved an Inter-Ministerial Committee comprising the Federal Ministry of Marine and Blue Economy, the Nigerian Ports Authority and the Nigeria Ports Economic Regulatory Agency. The committee, he said, would prepare a Port Business Continuity and Cargo Flow Management Plan to coordinate construction phases, vessel scheduling, cargo evacuation, truck movement and the use of alternative ports and transport systems. Oyetola added that the Lagos ports upgrade was part of a wider maritime development programme that included the approved modernisation of Onne, Rivers, Delta and Calabar ports. Also speaking, Oyedele said the project would help reduce the cost of doing business, improve the competitiveness of Nigerian products and support economic growth. He described the financing arrangement as Nigeria’s largest sovereign export credit transaction since 2009 and the first project in the country for Poland’s Export Credit Insurance Corporation, KUKE. Oyedele said the transaction reflected international confidence in Nigeria’s economic reforms and assured stakeholders of the government’s commitment to timely approvals, transparency and a stable operating environment. The Managing Director of the Nigerian Ports Authority, Dr Abubakar Dantsoho, described the groundbreaking as a landmark in the authority’s history. He said the NPA would ensure that the project was executed in line with approved designs, engineering standards and contractual timelines, while maintaining technical supervision, quality assurance and coordination. Dantsoho also pledged attention to safety, environmental standards and the uninterrupted operation of the ports during construction. The ceremony was attended by Poland’s Deputy Foreign Minister, Marcin Bosacki; Polish Ambassador to Nigeria, Michal Cygan; and the British Deputy High Commissioner in Lagos, Jonny Baxter, as well as contractors, international financing partners and maritime industry stakeholders. Apapa and Tin Can Island are among Nigeria’s principal maritime gateways, handling a substantial share of the country’s import and export cargo. However, ageing infrastructure, congestion, lengthy cargo clearance and evacuation processes, and high logistics costs have frequently been cited as challenges affecting port efficiency. The modernisation is intended to improve the capacity and operational performance of the Lagos ports at a time when African countries are seeking to expand trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area.
